precepts.text: Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. The leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy; the leaven of the Pharisees is sin. When you keep reading it says, for they say and do not. So the leaven in the scriptures is really going into sin. The days of unleavened bread that we are celebrating right now represent us being without sin.
precepts.point: Offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with leaven, for this liketh you, O ye children of Israel. We were offering our offerings of thanksgiving with leaven, meaning with sin, and thinking that is acceptable to God. You cannot give God offerings while you are in the midst of sin. The Lord said, I do not deal with that.
precepts.why:
Amos rebukes Israel: “offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with leaven, and proclaim and publish the free offerings: for this liketh you, O ye children of Israel”. Christ shows what that leaven is: “Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees”.

The leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy; the leaven of the Pharisees is sin. Christ is saying, be careful of the sins of the Pharisees, for they say and do not. So the leaven in the scriptures is really going into sin, and leaven is not only bread with yeast in it; it is something much more symbolic.

That is what Amos exposes. We were offering our thanksgiving with leaven, with sin, and thinking that was acceptable to God. You cannot be in the midst of sin and give God thanks offerings. The Lord said, I don't work with that, I don't deal with that. That's how you black people is: in the midst of sin and coming to me with offerings.

So the days of unleavened bread we are celebrating represent us being without sin. The soul that has leaven in it for those seven days is cut off, and that is damnation. It is going into something much heavier: the days of unleavened bread are us fixing ourselves right now, getting rid of the leaven, the sins you are battling, trying to become a better person, so that when the Lord returns our souls are not cut off.

precepts.text: I have smitten you with blasting and mildew; your gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees the palmerworm devoured: famine.
precepts.point: Amos shows what the blasting and mildew go into: famine, pestilence after the manner of Egypt, young men slain with the sword, death and destruction.

note.label: Deuteronomy 28: The Blessings and the Curses That Identify Israel

precepts.why:
“The Lord shall smite thee with a consumption, and with a fever, and with an inflammation, and with an extreme burning, and with the sword, and with blasting, and with mildew”. Amos shows what the blasting and the mildew go into: “I have smitten you with blasting and mildew: when your gardens and your vineyards and your fig trees and your olive trees increased, the palmerworm devoured them”. Gardens, vineyards, fig trees and olive trees all devoured: that is famine.

And after all of it, “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the Lord.” The curses of Deuteronomy 28 are the Most High's own hand, sent to turn Israel back, and they pursue until we return or perish.

precepts.text: I have sent among you the pestilence after the manner of Egypt; your young men have I slain with the sword; yet have ye not returned unto me.
precepts.point: Amos shows what the blasting and mildew go into: famine, pestilence after the manner of Egypt, young men slain with the sword, death and destruction.

note.label: Deuteronomy 28: The Blessings and the Curses That Identify Israel

precepts.why:
“The Lord shall make the pestilence cleave unto thee”: diseases. Amos shows the same hand at work: “I have sent among you the pestilence after the manner of Egypt: your young men have I slain with the sword, and have taken away your horses; and I have made the stink of your camps to come up unto your nostrils”. The pestilence, the sword, young men slain, death and destruction: exactly what Deuteronomy says shall “pursue thee until thou perish.”

“yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the Lord.” The pestilence and the sword are sent by the Most High himself, and they keep pursuing because Israel has not returned to him.

Hear this word, ye kine of Bashan in the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor, crush the needy, and say to their masters, bring and let us drink. The common theme here is the oppression of the poor, the needy, and the righteous.

points: The Lord God has sworn by his holiness that the day shall come when he will take you away with hooks and your posterity with fishhooks, and you shall go out at the breaches, every cow at that which is before her, and cast them into the palace.

note.label: Amos 4: Prepare to Meet Thy God

points: Come to Bethel and transgress, at Gilgal multiply transgression, bring your sacrifices every morning and your tithes after three years, and offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving with leaven, for this liketh you, O children of Israel.

note.label: Amos 4: Prepare to Meet Thy God

points: The Most High gave them cleanness of teeth and want of bread in all their places, withheld the rain three months before harvest, and caused it to rain on one city and not another, so people wandered from city to city to drink and were not satisfied, yet they did not return unto him.

note.label: Amos 4: Prepare to Meet Thy God

points: He smote them with blasting and mildew, the palmerworm devoured their gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees, he sent pestilence after the manner of Egypt, slew their young men with the sword, and overthrew some of them as he overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, yet they did not return unto him. The Lord blesses us and withholds and blesses again, and Israel is still not satisfied, forgetting the good times when everything turns bad.

note.label: Amos 4: Prepare to Meet Thy God

points: Therefore thus will he do unto Israel, and because he will do this, prepare to meet thy God, O Israel.

note.label: Amos 4: Prepare to Meet Thy God

points: He forms the mountains, creates the wind, declares unto man his thought, makes the morning darkness, and treads upon the high places of the earth; the Lord the God of hosts is his name. He treads upon the high places, the other nations and their power, being over all of it. You can use this as a precept when someone wants to play the name game with you, for there are many different titles.
